questions.q: Why is a vectorized numpy operation usually faster than a Python loop?
options: It works on a whole block of same-type numbers in compiled code
It skips half of the values
why: Correct. The loop runs in fast compiled code, not one Python step at a time.
No. The results are the same.

questions.why: a > 4 keeps 6 and 8. Their sum is 14.

questions.q: x = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 5.0]). What is np.isnan(x).sum()?
questions.why: np.isnan gives [False, True, False]. The sum counts one True.

questions.q: table has shape (100, 4): 100 days and 4 sensors. You want the mean of each sensor. Which call?
why: Correct. axis=0 goes down the rows, so you get 4 values, one per column.
That gives 100 values, one per day.
That gives one number for the whole table.

questions.q: You compute (table - table.mean(axis=1)) with table of shape (5, 3). It fails. Why, and what is the fix?
options: The row means have shape (5,), which does not match 3 columns. Use keepdims=True.
You must convert the table to a list first.
why: Correct. Shape (5,) is compared with 3 from the right. keepdims=True gives (5, 1), which broadcasts.
numpy can subtract arrays of compatible shapes.
Lists are slower and not needed.

questions.q: A sensor array has some nan values. You need the average of the valid ones. Which call?
why: This returns nan when any value is nan.
This returns nan and also divides by the wrong count.

questions.q: Which expression is True when x is nan?
why: nan is never equal to anything, even to itself. This is always False.
